name: The Grandfather Paradox
statement: The grandfather paradox asks what happens if a time traveler kills their own grandfather before their parent is conceived.
statementAccent: kills their own grandfather before their parent is conceived
meaning: It is the classic illustration of a "consistency paradox" in time-travel logic: if the traveller prevents their grandfather from fathering their parent, the traveller is never born, so they could never have travelled back to commit the act, so the grandfather survives, so the traveller is born after all (an endless contradiction). It is used to argue either that backward time travel to a mutable past is logically impossible, or to motivate principles that forbid such contradictions.
mechanism: The paradox arises from assuming the past can be causally altered by an actor whose own existence depends on the unaltered past, creating a closed causal loop with no consistent set of events. Proposed resolutions include the Novikov self-consistency principle, only self-consistent actions are physically possible, and the many-worlds view, in which the action spins off a divergent timeline rather than altering the traveller’s own.

examples.text: French writer René Barjavel’s 1943 novel "Le Voyageur Imprudent" is credited as an early and influential fictional presentation of the grandfather-paradox scenario.
The concept appeared earlier in Nathaniel Schachner’s 1933 story "Ancestral Voices," and variants were discussed in readers’ letters to Amazing Stories in the 1920s.

Physicist Igor Novikov proposed the self-consistency principle, under which any action a traveller takes must already have been part of history, so a would-be grandfather-killer would always be thwarted in some consistent way.

whyItMatters: The paradox is a central test case in the philosophy of time and in physics discussions of closed timelike curves permitted by general relativity, forcing precise thinking about causality, free will, and logical consistency in any theory that allows travel to the past.
limits: It specifically targets a mutable, changeable past; it does not automatically apply to models (Novikov self-consistency, or a fixed block universe) where the past cannot be altered by definition, so its force depends on which theory of time travel is assumed. It is a thought experiment, not an observed phenomenon.
misreadings: It is often mistaken for a proof that all time travel is impossible, when it more precisely shows only that travel permitting free alteration of a fixed past leads to contradiction: travel compatible with self-consistency or branching timelines is not automatically ruled out.
origin: Early versions circulated in 1920s Amazing Stories letters and Schachner’s 1933 story; the scenario received its canonical fictional treatment in René Barjavel’s 1943 novel "Le Voyageur Imprudent." It is a thought-experiment label, not an eponymous law.
